statement: In healthy volunteers and women with insomnia in driving studies, evidence is insufficient to say whether next-morning impairment after benzodiazepine sleeping pills fades over the first week of nightly use: in a network meta-analysis, residual effects seemed to fall with repeated use, which the authors cautiously put down to tolerance, except for flurazepam, which impaired driving after a few nights (standardized mean difference 1.65, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.32) and lormetazepam's estimate after two nights (0.44, -0.23 to 1.10) was no smaller than after one night (0.43) (Fornaro et al., 2024, accepted manuscript); in on-road studies summarized in a narrative review, impairment after flurazepam increased slightly over 7 nights, impairment after nitrazepam did not diminish over a week, and impairment after lormetazepam at its higher dose peaked after 4 nights and then declined (Vermeeren, 2004, second-hand). No study followed people for more than about two weeks. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: It is not known whether the next-morning effects of these sleeping pills wear off with nightly use; for some they lasted or grew over a week.
population: Healthy adult volunteers and, in some on-road studies, women with insomnia who had used sleeping pills before
exposure: Nightly use of a benzodiazepine sleeping pill for two nights to about a week (flurazepam, lormetazepam, nitrazepam; study doses on the study cards)
comparator: Placebo nights, and the first night of use
outcome: Next-morning driving impairment (weaving) over successive nights
magnitude: Network meta-analysis, end of repeated dosing: flurazepam 1.65 (95% CI 0.98 to 2.32) against placebo; lormetazepam 0.44 (-0.23 to 1.10), against 0.43 (-0.23 to 1.09) after one dose. On-road series (second-hand): flurazepam impairment slightly larger over 7 nights and still present after the first night without it; nitrazepam unchanged from night 2 to night 7; lormetazepam at the higher dose largest after 4 nights; temazepam soft capsules and lormetazepam at the lower dose without residual effects all week.

evidence.locator: 3.3 Next-morning driving impairment, study endpoint, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: At the study endpoint (k = 9, n = 806), flurazepam was worse than placebo (SMD 1.65, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.32) while the other evaluated compounds, including lormetazepam, did not differ significantly from placebo (the zopiclone control aside).

evidence.extracted: Lormetazepam against placebo: 0.43 (95% CI -0.23 to 1.09) after one dose and 0.44 (-0.23 to 1.10) at the end of repeated dosing; flurazepam at endpoint 1.65 (0.98 to 2.32) against placebo and 1.23 (0.52 to 1.94) against zopiclone.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Fornaro_2024_ResidualDrivingNMA..pdf (accepted manuscript, author Word version with pages 1-26, not the typeset article), read in full

evidence.extracted: The authors suggest that repeated administration seemed to reduce residual effects, likely through tolerance, except for flurazepam, whose effects may need more time to build tolerance.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Fornaro_2024_ResidualDrivingNMA..pdf (accepted manuscript, author Word version with pages 1-26, not the typeset article), read in full

evidence.extracted: In driving tests over a week of nightly use, impairment after flurazepam slightly increased over 7 nights and persisted after the first washout night; impairment after nitrazepam did not diminish from the second to the seventh night; lormetazepam soft capsules at the higher dose were most impairing after 4 nights; temazepam soft capsules and lormetazepam at the lower dose showed no residual effects throughout a week.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

evidence.extracted: According to the meta-analysis cited by the author, the share of impaired performance measures fell with repeated use, more quickly for shorter-acting drugs, suggesting tolerance that may be incomplete and may take longer than a week.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Benzodiazepines/Vermeeren_2004_ResidualEffectsHypnotics.pdf (published version, CNS Drugs 2004;18:297-328), read in full

risk_of_bias.note: Few small trials, some second-hand through a narrative review largely from the author's group.

inconsistency.note: Accumulation with flurazepam, no change with nitrazepam, a rise and fall with lormetazepam at the higher dose.

indirectness.note: Healthy volunteers and some women with insomnia; the short durations are stated in the claim.

imprecision.note: Lormetazepam's intervals span no effect to large effects; one trial per drug.

grade.reasoning: Randomized crossover trials start high; downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, giving very low. The network meta-analysis and the narrative review share the flurazepam on-road studies, so they are not independent. Status mixed: drugs behaved differently. The tolerance seen for some non-benzodiazepine sleep medicines in the same network is not evidence for benzodiazepines.
